utterances.text: I did not have a person acting as deputy commander because the command of the Operative Zone in structure differed from the structure of the command of the 3rd Corps, but, of course, my subordinate, according to the military hierarchy, was my chief of staff, Franjo Nakic, and the 3rd Corps did have a deputy commander of the 3rd Corps. He was Mr. Dzemo Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Fine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The next conclusion was that the centre in Busovaca --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, did this difference in the structures of the HVO and the BiH produce any practical difficulties of administration for one side or the other?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, certainly it did cause difficulty in practical terms because for me this meant that my headquarters would be left without a chief of staff for the ensuing period which meant that I was short of staff anyway and now I had to assign my chief of staff to another task. That is one thing. Secondly, in the 3rd Corps, the chief of staff retained his original function and his regular assignments whereas the commander of the 3rd Corps appointed his deputy to the joint operations centre. That is the only difference. So one command was left without a chief of staff and the other had one in real terms and formally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: For the conduct of combat operations, will you tell the Court who is the second person in importance in both the 3rd Corps and the operative centre?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Everywhere it is the chief of staff. That is the centre where all information is gathered, where all decisions are taken, and the chief of staff, in fact, prepares all decisions for the commander and reports to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Since we have the conclusions in writing, I would suggest that document 339 be shown to you, and we should like to distribute copies of this new document, and these documents refer to the conclusions of the meeting in Zenica. The only thing is that one document was by those who signed the agreement and the other one is an internal document from the HVO. So will you please give a copy to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D547.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, please look at the document D339 and tell us, please, whether those are the conclusions of the meeting that you were referring to today. This is an old document, D339. I am referring first to document D339. Does it contain the conclusions of the meeting in Zenica, the meeting that you just described?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they contain all the conclusions, but there is one addition that I had taken note of -- I cannot see it in this document. This addition was proposed by Colonel Stewart to the chairman, Thebault, that is, the chief of the European Monitoring Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What did it relate to?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When all these conclusions that are contained in the document had been dictated, I described how they came about, but after that, Colonel Stewart took a military map and showed it to the head of the European Mission, Mr. Thebault, who then gave the floor to Colonel Stewart, and the HVO and the commander of the 3rd Corps were required, in relation to the UNPROFOR base in Nova Bila, that an area around the base, 500 metres around the base, should be demilitarised; in other words, that all military effects should be withdrawn in an area of 500 metres diameter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did the BH army do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If it had done so, which area would it have had to evacuate?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Most of Grbavica and a greater part of Divjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Please look now at the new document that we have just distributed, D547, which is the agreement, and pay attention to the signatures on the last page. Do you perhaps recognise any of those signatures?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I recognise the signature of Brigadier Petkovic, General Sefer Halilovic, and General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We are not going to read the document. It is self-explanatory in terms of the conclusions at the Zenica meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I ask this question, General? In this document, paragraph 3, fifth line refers to "both deputy commanders." Should I understand that on your side to be referring to your chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. I did not have a deputy, and that was a well-known fact to the chairman, Mr. Thebault, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. So this meeting was over, you went back to your headquarters. Do you recall whether the fighting had abated -- or, rather, you didn't tell us whether you went to the phone and made phone calls to certain units, you and Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Both of us were in a room which was on the same floor as the meeting room, and from one telephone, the commander of the 3rd Corps, Enver Hadzihasanovic, called his chief of staff, and later I called Slavko Marin too, and we dictated the decisions of this meeting through an order, and we both asked that the orders be sent to our subordinates on the ground straightaway. I told Slavko Marin that he should not wait for my return from Zenica to Vitez but that he should immediately prepare this order and have it sent out to certain units, this order on the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. How did you go back? How did you return to the hotel, to your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was quite late in the evening, perhaps about 23.00, I'm not too sure. The same way I went to Zenica, that is to say, with three UN armoured vehicles and our vehicle was in the middle and, again, we went to the back door of the hotel, and I think that somewhere near Kaonik, that part of the road, there was sporadic gunfire, but I'm not sure, and I couldn't see a thing because, again, the visors were down and it was night-time and we were going back to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you saw Marin and did you briefly tell him what you heard in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was with Slavko Marin, and I conveyed to him the substance that Dzemo Merdan had communicated to me, and I told Slavko Marin that Dzemo Merdan had established at the meeting that there were quite a few casualties, including civilians, and he mentioned a figure of around 500. I asked Slavko Marin also whether he had received a report and whether we have received any information whatsoever on that figure, and Slavko then said that we didn't. Slavko also told me about what had happened in the school of Dubravica and at Impregnacija and how the front line fell and how it was recaptured again. After that, I went to rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the 21st of April, you had another meeting with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Nova Bila but only at 12.00. Tell me, what kind of information did you receive in the morning of the 21st of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Information was coming in, into the operations staff, and around 2.00, again it became evident that the forces of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were on the move. At 3.00, we received information from the Vitez Brigade that fire had been opened against the positions at Kratine and Nadioci from Kuber, and we received the recording of a conversation from the head of the Military Intelligence Service, and I quote: "We have to take Vitez regardless of the price involved and the sacrifices involved."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who said that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was a conversation between the commander of the units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina that the Military Intelligence Service had intercepted and recorded probably via radio communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That day, in the morning, disturbing news also came in from Travnik; right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. At 10.30, we received information that the situation in Travnik was very critical and that the snipers of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina are operating in the area of Kalibunar and also they are shooting at Croat apartments and that two women, two Croat women, were hit by snipers of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the town of Travnik. Tensions were very high and, around 11.30, a delegation arrived, a delegation of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the Vitez Hotel, and they were escorted either by the European Monitoring Mission and UNPROFOR or only by UNPROFOR. On this delegation was Mr. Sefer Halilovic, Stjepan Siber, the deputy chief of staff of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then Mr. Vehbija Karic, Mr. Dzemo Merdan, and on behalf of the HVO, there was Brigadier Petkovic, chief of the main staff of the HVO, and there was Mr. Lucic and Mr. Bandic, and I was present too. It was a brief conversation just before the meeting in Nova Bila in which we mainly discussed the agreement that was signed last night, on the 20th of April, 1993. After that, we set out for Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How did you do that? Could you tell us the mode of transport?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, we were transported separately, escorted by UNPROFOR, of course. That is how we were transported to Nova Bila to a house that is across the street from the UN base. It was a civilian house that was rented by the European Monitoring Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please tell us of the content of the discussion of this meeting, briefly?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Before the meeting, I told Brigadier Petkovic about the disturbing news I had about operations in Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak, and I said that the agreement was not being enforced yet and that it was obvious that either information did not come in or perhaps it was not even sent. I mean information regarding the signing of this agreement between the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO. At the meeting on the 21st of April, at 12.00, there was the head of the European Monitoring Mission, Mr. Thebault, and another high official of the European Monitoring Mission. I imagine that his name was Mr. Ford, but I'm not too sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you talking about the 21st or the 24th of April? I'm a bit lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The 21st.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, the 21st of April, 1993, at 12.00. The meeting in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that meeting, after he took the floor, Brigadier Petkovic said we could not or did not wish to stop combat operations from last night until now and the members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina have not only not stopped combat operations but have expanded military operations, combat operations, and at the moment, Busovaca and Kiseljak are being attacked and also there are operations taking place in Vitez. Then he said, General Petkovic, I mean, said, "Since last night, you have been phoning units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the attacks, instead of being stopped, are only spreading from Travnik to Kiseljak. The village of Badnje and the region around the village of Badnje was attacked by you and taken militarily." He was referring to the attack for the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Thebault, the chairman, said, "Commanders," as he was addressing Sefer and Brigadier Petkovic, "it is your credibility that is at stake now. Let us enforce on the ground what we signed last night. If you're not in a position to do that, then it is going to be very difficult to find a solution. The one who does not wish to enforce this should get up and leave this meeting. The situation is far too serious today for us not to do a thing." After that, General Halilovic took the floor, the chief of the main staff of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who said, "Combat operations are a consequence of the situation at the front because units are still in combat contact. In Travnik, in Novi Travnik, there are two-way operations of groups of HVO and of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak, the units are in combat contact, and it is very difficult to keep the situation under control and bring it to a halt all of a sudden. I am prepared to go to these lines of conflict straightaway and to solve all the problems right there."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, General, Sefer Halilovic, the first soldier of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so to speak, if we do not mention the head of state, he said that he would go to the front line and resolve problems. Wouldn't it be more correct from a military point of view for two commanders, Halilovic of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Petkovic of HVO, to issue orders, every one of them to his subordinate, Petkovic to you and Halilovic to Hadzihasanovic, and then, according to firm military subordination, a firm chain of command, shouldn't there be a cease-fire and wouldn't it be normal to enforce the orders of the commander in chief rather than have the commander in chief go to the trenches?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's what they did at the meeting of the 20th of April. Petkovic ordered me, and Halilovic ordered Enver to get up and to go immediately and call our subordinates and to dictate orders on the cessation of combat operations from that hotel, both of us, and I know that Enver called Mekic and dictated the conclusions of this meeting from the 20th of April, 1993 to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who is Mekic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The head of the staff of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you call your own people?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I called Slavko Marin and I dictated it to him, and I told him immediately to send this order out and not to wait for me to come back but that he should send it out to the ground immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How do you explain the fact that this is not sufficient, that these orders were not obeyed, but now Sefer Halilovic, who is the chief of general staff of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, would have to go to trenches to see that the cease-fire is enforced right there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly there were problems in the functioning of the chain of command, both on the side of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and also from the further proceedings of the meeting. Both the head of the general staff of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the head of the main staff of the HVO indeed did go to the front line to see that combat operations were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please proceed? Did Halilovic say anything else?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Sefer Halilovic addressed Brigadier Petkovic at the time. He said, "Petkovic, this morning your artillery fired at Zenica. Three or four shells fell." And I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is the 21st of April, 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. After that, Petkovic said again that it was not the HVO that was firing, he established that Busovaca and Kiseljak were under attack at present and from the positions of Kuber, Kacuni, and the village of Badnje, and he said, "Halilovic, you can stop these attacks." Mr. Ford -- I mean the gentleman who I think is called Ford -- asked to take the floor then, he greeted all the participants in this meeting, and he suggested that we should not waste our energy on that that has been but that we should concentrate on that which will come. The conclusions after this meeting were that combat operations should be stopped and that the movement of all members of the European Community and UNPROFOR should be guaranteed freedom of movement and to create a neutral zone between HVO units and BH army units, and in that neutral zone, only UNPROFOR forces, that is to say, the British battalion forces, should be the only ones patrolling, and also to guarantee the safety of the civilian population with special emphasis on the Bosniak Muslims of Vitez and the Croats of Zenica and that public law and order should be improved and the institutions in charge of this should make every effort in that direction. Also, support was given to the joint commission that was supposed to work on all these tasks and common problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the basis of that meeting, you wrote an order, and I would like D336 to be handed out, please, D336. Please look at the document. First its general appearance. Is it an order which you issued to your forces after the meeting in Nova Bila, the meeting you have just described?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote this order personally, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You addressed the order to the chief of the main staff of the HVO, for his information, to the European Monitoring Mission, to the United Nations command, and to all immediately subordinated commanders. Could you explain to us, are you giving orders to the European Monitoring Mission and the British Battalion, and why did you put them together with your immediately subordinated commanders? Could you explain the actual process of writing this order?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course. It should have said "for the information of the monitoring mission and also for the attention of the United Nations command," so this was probably an error on the part of the typists. I never issued any orders to the monitoring mission and the UN command at Nova Bila, but in each of the points, I indicated who was responsible for implementing specific tasks. It was my habit that any agreement reached with representatives of the BH army should be regulated through an order so that we would know exactly what we needed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the heading, it says: "Implementation of the agreement between units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO. Order," and then it says: "At 12.00 on the 21st of April, 1993, a meeting was held in Nova Bila," on the basis of which you are issuing an order. However, it is quite clear in the text that the meeting was held on the 21st of April at 12.00, but in the heading where the date is indicated, it says: "9.10."

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is this an error, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, clearly this is an error on the part of the typist. We often had such mistakes, partly due to my extremely illegible handwriting and perhaps because of the fatigue of the typist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In any event, the meeting started at 12.00. How long did it last for?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I couldn't say with precision but certainly not less than two hours. Perhaps longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This order, when could it have been written?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the afternoon, perhaps around 21.00, 21.10. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Will you please take note of point 6, which I'm going to read: "The commanders of the HVO brigades are obliged to guarantee full security of the civilian Muslim people and all other peoples in their zone of responsibility, and the competent bodies of the HVO are obliged to ensure public law and order, especially with regard to the Muslim inhabitants of the town of Vitez and the Croats of the town of Zenica." Could you please explain this sentence, why you wrote it down? What was your purpose?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the meeting, we had discussed this problem and the chain reaction that things had. Anything bad that would happen to Croats in Zenica and Travnik in an area under the control of the BH army would have a chain reaction in the areas of Vitez, when the victims in that case were usually Muslims. That is why I insisted that one of the points should reflect our effort to prevent any violence towards Croats in Zenica and towards Muslims in Vitez, in order to stop these chain reactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But you cannot have any influence over the situation in Zenica, can you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly I could not, especially not after the 18th of April, when the Croatian Defence Council in Zenica ceased to function and when I personally had no access to Zenica. But I knew that all the trouble coming with the exiled Croats from Zenica, who were finding accommodation in Vitez, was reflected upon the Muslims of Vitez, who later became the object or victim of persecution by those Croats from Zenica, and I wanted to interrupt that chain of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to point 8 of that order. Let me read it and then ask my question. "Brigade commanders are obliged to issue written orders to their subordinated commanders on the basis of this order and to start implementing it. They are to send one copy of their order to the Vitez Operative Zone command of Central Bosnia." Tell us, why did you put this sentence in your order?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Ever since the January conflicts, there were quite a lot of problems with the functioning of the chain of command, and we would form a special set of documents for any agreement. After such an agreement was reached, we would have orders, as well as orders issued by the immediate subordinates, because sometimes it was simply not clear to the European monitors that we would order one thing and something quite different would happen on the ground. That is why we wanted to make sure that the commanders would issue orders on the basis of our orders and that they would try to ensure the implementation of those orders on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting you, Mr. Nobilo. General, is this the first time you used this method of trying to have feedback on your orders or did you try other times before?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We had done so before. It was not the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm in a dilemma now as to how long we are going to go on working today, this afternoon. Are we working until 6.00 or until 5.30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will work until 5.30. That is the reason why I did not allow us to take a break. Maybe the accused is very tired. I mean, it's his right to be tired. If that is the case, of course, we can take a short break. General Blaskic, do you feel able to continue until 5.30 without a break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I can, Mr. President. It is up to you. I can. I'm at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well then. We are going to work for another fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Having finished with this order, we can go on to the 22nd of April, 1993. Will you please tell Their Honours how that day began? What did you focus on? What were you doing on the 22nd of April, 1993? What were your main concerns?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On that day, the 22nd of April, 1993, I had a meeting with the commanders, and the subject of the meeting was implementation of the order on the implementation of the agreement of the 21st of April, 1993, and we mainly discussed the points and the contents of this order, as well as the methods of its implementation. I also requested special guarantees for the safety of civilians, and I stressed to the commanders that this was one of our priority tasks. I also instructed the assistant for information to put in order all the information that we had received so far regarding civilian casualties, that is, all information and our reactions to that problem. I also tasked the assistant for security at this meeting to take preventive measures to protect civilians, and I also gave instructions to the head of operations to work on a plan of work for the command. At that meeting, I also discussed the plan on the separation of forces, which was perhaps one of the fundamental points of this order of the 21st of April, because the plan was for the entire area between Zenica, Vitez, Kaonik, and Lasva to be demilitarised or, rather, for only UNPROFOR to be present there and to patrol the area. This would mean the withdrawal of the forces of the BH army towards Zenica, that is, from Kuber and the lines they had captured, and also the withdrawal of the HVO towards Vitez and Busovaca. I was also informed on that day by the head of the Military Intelligence Service that movement had been prohibited for all HVO motor vehicles, including ambulances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you came across, for the first time, different criteria of the UNHCR, the International Red Cross, and UNPROFOR on this day. Can you explain to the Court what kind of criteria these were and how they differed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'll try to explain, though I must say at first I found it rather complicated. The position of the UNHCR, and I'm speaking only of the area where I was the commander, that we commanders have to provide full security for the civilian population, and any movement or any resettlement of civilians and their movement from their places of residence constituted ethnic cleansing, according to the criteria of the UNHCR. The position of the International Red Cross and UNPROFOR was that we commanders had to ensure full freedom of movement for all civilians living in the area under the HVO and probably the area controlled by the BH army, I assumed, though I didn't know that. So that these two positions were in contradiction with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In a situation of a civil war and inter-ethnic conflict where we have two armies, each belonging to a different people, what does "freedom of movement" mean?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I tried to explain this to the International Red Cross, and I told them that if we were to allow freedom of movement, then no one would remain to live in Vitez. Vitez could be an example, but we also had data about Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Nobody would stay to live there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Neither the Muslims nor the Croats if, in an area of about six kilometres away, there were combat operations. Everybody would try to find a safer place to live. On the other hand, the position of the UNHCR, which was conveyed to me, was that the safety of civilians had to be fully guaranteed, and there should be no movement of the population. I was frequently confronted with certain arrangements made by the International Red Cross. Let me just give you an example. When the Croats held prisoner in Zenica were released, all of them, or at least a vast majority of them, 90 per cent perhaps, came to live in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you explain why the Croats from Zenica wanted to go to Vitez when there is fighting there too?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Out of fear for their personal safety. Some of them were mobilised, or they assumed they would be mobilised by the BH army, and taken to the front line between the HVO and the BH army; some, that they would be taken in custody subsequently for interrogation; and when they had a chance, according to the criteria of the International Red Cross, to opt for a place where they wanted to live, those prisoners chose for their next place of residence Busovaca and Vitez, and their families stayed on in Zenica, in their own apartments and homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, I understand you to be saying that if there was freedom of movement, all the Croats and all the Muslims in Vitez would have left Vitez because of the occurrence of armed conflict in the vicinity. How do you reconcile that with the fact that Croats left Zenica and came to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, having to choose from two bad solutions, and this is my assumption and I spoke to them, they chose the one that was least bad. When I said that both Croats and Muslims would have left, I remember that in March, the second half of March, I received information from Busovaca, I think it was an information from the IPD, Information Propaganda Service, that about 60 complete Croatian families from Busovaca had reported to the Busovaca police station and about 74 to 80 Muslim families saying that they wanted to leave Busovaca, which means both Croats and Muslims. Of course, some wanted to leave to third countries, that is, leave Bosnia-Herzegovina entirely, whereas others wanted to go to Zenica or other areas under the control of their army because there was a danger that Busovaca would fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In a situation when it is not possible to abandon a country at war, everyone did not have such a chance, what did each ethnic group decide? Where did they prefer to go if they did not have the possibility of leaving the war zone?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They went where the army of their entity had control: the Croats to the areas under the control of the HVO and the Bosniak Muslims to the areas under the control of the BH army. The situation was particularly grave when male members of families -- this was not a question of a hundred people. On one day, we received about 300 military conscripts from Zenica, whereas all their families were left behind in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What happened then? What happened with those Croats who came to Vitez and their families stayed behind in areas under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They tried to do everything they could to have their families join them. Some sought to do so through the mediation of the International Red Cross, and I had a talk with a representative of the International Red Cross on the 22nd of April when I became aware of the existence of these different criteria. According to one set of criteria, every movement was assessed as ethnic cleansing, and according to others, I had to ensure full freedom of movement. Others, apart from applying to the International Red Cross, sought out personal arrangements. They would knock at the door of a Bosniak Muslim whom they knew and they would ask his families, because there were similar situations on the other side, that is, released Bosniak Muslims who chose to live in Zenica and Travnik also sought to achieve reunification of their families who were left behind in Vitez. So such personal arrangements were made independently of international organisations. As far as I know, a civilian agency was formed, attached to the civilian authorities in Vitez municipality, for mediation in the exchange of apartments and reunification of families.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What did you tell the representatives of the International Red Cross and UNPROFOR? What was your position? What did you ask of them?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, I said that the UNHCR had another criterion and that was that it joined in the evacuation of Bosniak Muslims and Croats from territories controlled by the army of Republika Srpska, and there were cases of population resettlement from the territories under the control of Republika Srpska army --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us say that once again because the transcript -- there's an error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, this is a complex question you're about to put to the witness, so maybe it would be a better idea to go back to this question tomorrow when we start working again in the morning. I think that we all want the witness to tell us exactly how these negotiations went with the UNHCR and with the International Red Cross. We all want to know exactly what the consequences of these negotiations were for the populations. That's a crucial issue. I think the witness is a bit tired. We will go over this point tomorrow morning. The hearing is adjourned. We will meet tomorrow morning at 10.00. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 5.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 11th day of March, 1999 at 10.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
